questions.q: Why isn't a successful .sqlproj build enough proof that a migration works?
options: Building only confirms the schema is internally consistent — it doesn't confirm the migration actually runs correctly against real data
A successful build is fully sufficient and no further testing is ever needed
SSDT builds always fail even for correct migrations
Building tests every possible query the application could ever run
questions.explain: CI's build step validates references and syntax, not runtime behavior against actual data.

questions.q: What is the spin-up, migrate, test, tear-down pattern?
options: Creating a fresh, disposable test database for a pipeline run, applying migrations, running smoke tests, then destroying it
Permanently reusing one shared test database across every pipeline run indefinitely
Manually testing changes by hand on the production server
A pattern used only for application code, never for databases
questions.explain: A genuinely disposable database, created and destroyed each run, ensures a clean, repeatable test every time.

questions.q: What is a smoke test, in the context of a database pipeline?
options: A small, fast set of sanity checks confirming the basics work, not exhaustive testing
A performance stress test that floods the database with maximum load
A full audit of every row in every table
A manual code review conducted by a human DBA
questions.explain: Smoke tests are meant to be quick, catching obviously broken migrations or objects, not providing exhaustive coverage.

questions.q: Why does using a fresh test database every pipeline run give a more reliable test than reusing one long-lived test database?
options: It avoids leftover test data or state from a prior failed run masking or causing false results, proving migrations work from a clean slate
Fresh databases run migrations faster due to less disk fragmentation
SQL Server requires a new database for every migration script
It has no real benefit; either approach is equally reliable
questions.explain: A clean slate each run matches what an actual brand-new environment would experience, avoiding contamination from prior runs.

questions.q: What happens if a smoke test fails during the pipeline?
options: The pipeline stops there, and the change never reaches production, with the failure tied to the specific commit that caused it
The pipeline ignores the failure and deploys to production anyway
The test database is kept alive indefinitely for manual inspection
The migration is automatically edited to fix the failure
questions.explain: A failed smoke test halts the pipeline, surfacing the problem immediately rather than letting it reach production.
